findings.title: Your OpenAI key is visible to every visitor

ghost_path.story: A customer walks up to the shop.
ghost_path.why: Every request starts here. The app cannot trust anything the visitor sends.
ghost_path.code: No code runs yet. The visitor only has what the public website gives them.

ghost_path.data: the page and its public settings
ghost_path.story: They look through the shop window. Only things meant for customers are on display.
ghost_path.why: The front end is shipped to every visitor's browser, so everything in it is public.
ghost_path.code: Pets.tsx runs in the browser and can only use values that are safe to show.

ghost_path.data: requests sent from the back room
ghost_path.story: Calls to the outside supplier should be made from the back room, where the key never leaves the building.
ghost_path.why: api.openai.com trusts whoever holds the key, so only the server should hold it.
ghost_path.code: A server-side function adds the key to the request, so the browser never sees it.

attack_path.story: Someone with bad intentions walks up to the same shop.
attack_path.why: Every request starts here. The app cannot trust anything the visitor sends.
attack_path.code: No code runs yet. The visitor only has what the public website gives them.

attack_path.story: They do not even go inside. They read everything taped to the shop window.
attack_path.why: The front end is shipped to every visitor's browser, so everything in it is public.
attack_path.code: Pets.tsx is bundled with every VITE_ or NEXT_PUBLIC_ value the build can see.

attack_path.story: There it is: the key under the doormat. VITE_OPENAI_API_KEY is written right where anyone can pick it up.
attack_path.why: A key that pays for or controls an outside service must stay on the server. Once it is in the browser, it belongs to everyone.
attack_path.code: .env line 4 defines VITE_OPENAI_API_KEY. Build tools copy public-prefixed values into the JavaScript every visitor downloads.

attack_path.story: They walk across the road to the supplier and order on your account.
attack_path.why: api.openai.com cannot tell your app from the attacker: both send the same key.
attack_path.code: Any request with this key is billed to and trusted as your account.

fix.explanation: VITE_OPENAI_API_KEY is bundled into the website, so every visitor can copy it. Move the code that uses it into a Supabase Edge Function, store the key there as the secret OPENAI_API_KEY (without the public prefix), and call that function from the page. Then rotate the key in the provider's dashboard, because the old one has already been public.
fix.prompt: Lovable, please move VITE_OPENAI_API_KEY out of the front end. Create a Supabase Edge Function that reads the key from a secret called OPENAI_API_KEY and makes the outside API call, have the page call that function instead, and remove the key from .env. I will rotate the old key.

findings.title: Your Supabase admin key is in the browser code

ghost_path.story: A customer walks up to the shop.
ghost_path.why: Every request starts here. The app cannot trust anything the visitor sends.
ghost_path.code: No code runs yet. The visitor only has what the public website gives them.

ghost_path.story: Through the shop window they get a visitor badge that opens nothing by itself.
ghost_path.why: The anon key is safe to share because the vault's locks still apply to it.
ghost_path.code: from('adoption_requests') talks to Supabase with the anon key and the user's session.

ghost_path.story: They show their ID at the guard desk and get a pass with their name on it.
ghost_path.why: Supabase Auth ties every request to one user, so the locks know whose box to open.
ghost_path.code: auth.uid() is set from the signed-in user's token.

ghost_path.data: only this user's rows in profiles
ghost_path.story: At the vault, their pass opens their own box in profiles and nothing else.
ghost_path.why: Row level security checks every row against the user on the pass.
ghost_path.code: Policies on profiles filter rows by auth.uid().

attack_path.story: Someone with bad intentions walks up to the same shop.
attack_path.why: Every request starts here. The app cannot trust anything the visitor sends.
attack_path.code: No code runs yet. The visitor only has what the public website gives them.

attack_path.story: Taped to the shop window is the master key to the whole building.
attack_path.why: The service role key skips every lock in the database. It must never leave the server.
attack_path.code: src/lib/admin.ts line 6 puts VITE_SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY into front-end code, so the build ships it to every browser.

attack_path.data: the service role key instead of a user session
attack_path.story: With the master key they walk straight past the guard desk.
attack_path.why: The guard desk only matters for normal passes. The service role is not a user, so no one checks it.
attack_path.code: Requests made with the service role key bypass Supabase Auth and row level security.

attack_path.story: Every box in the vault opens, including profiles.
attack_path.why: Row level security is skipped entirely for the service role.
attack_path.code: With the service role, reads and writes on profiles ignore every policy.

attack_path.story: Every box in the vault opens, including adoption_requests.
attack_path.why: Row level security is skipped entirely for the service role.
attack_path.code: With the service role, reads and writes on adoption_requests ignore every policy.

fix.explanation: The Supabase service role key (VITE_SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY) is the master key: it ignores every database rule. Remove it from the front end and use the normal anon key there. Move anything that truly needs admin rights into an Edge Function, which can read the service role key from its own secrets. Then rotate the service role key in the Supabase dashboard (Project Settings, API), because the old one is public.
fix.prompt: Lovable, please remove the Supabase service role key (VITE_SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY) from all front-end code and use the anon key instead. If something needs admin access, move it into a Supabase Edge Function that checks the user is signed in. I will rotate the service role key in the Supabase dashboard.

findings.title: Any signed-in user can read everyone's adoption_requests

ghost_path.story: A customer walks up to the shop.
ghost_path.why: Every request starts here. The app cannot trust anything the visitor sends.
ghost_path.code: No code runs yet. The visitor only has what the public website gives them.

ghost_path.data: a request for rows in adoption_requests
ghost_path.story: In the shop window, the page asks the vault for this customer's records.
ghost_path.why: The browser can ask for anything, so the vault must decide what to hand over.
ghost_path.code: from('adoption_requests') queries adoption_requests with the public anon key.

ghost_path.story: They show their ID at the guard desk and get a pass with their name on it.
ghost_path.why: Supabase Auth identifies the user, so the vault knows whose rows are whose.
ghost_path.code: auth.uid() becomes the signed-in user's id for every query.

ghost_path.data: only rows where user_id is this user
ghost_path.story: At the vault, the lock on adoption_requests opens only their own box.
ghost_path.why: Row level security turns every query into 'only my rows'.
ghost_path.code: A policy like auth.uid() = user_id filters adoption_requests row by row.

attack_path.story: Someone with bad intentions walks up to the same shop.
attack_path.why: Every request starts here. The app cannot trust anything the visitor sends.
attack_path.code: No code runs yet. The visitor only has what the public website gives them.

attack_path.data: the public anon key and the table name
attack_path.story: The shop window shows them exactly which vault box the page uses.
attack_path.why: The anon key and table names are public by design. The lock is what keeps data safe.
attack_path.code: from('adoption_requests') reveals that the app reads adoption_requests.

attack_path.story: They sign up with any email. The guard desk gives a pass to anyone who asks.
attack_path.why: Being signed in proves who you are, not which rows are yours.
attack_path.code: Sign-up is open, so auth.uid() is not null for any account.

attack_path.data: a lock that opens for any pass
attack_path.story: Here is the broken lock: it checks that you have a pass, not that the box is yours.
attack_path.why: A read policy must compare the row's owner with the user. This one does not.
attack_path.code: Policy requests_select_authed on adoption_requests lets every signed-in user read every row.

attack_path.story: Every box in adoption_requests swings open, not just their own.
attack_path.why: Without an owner check, one query returns everyone's records.
attack_path.code: A plain select on adoption_requests returns all rows.

fix.explanation: The read rule on adoption_requests only checks that someone is signed in, so any account can read every row. Add a new migration that turns the lock on and lets each user read only rows where user_id is their own id.
fix.diff:
--- /dev/null
+++ b/supabase/migrations/0004_heist_lock_adoption_requests.sql
@@ -0,0 +1,4 @@
+drop policy "requests_select_authed" on public.adoption_requests;
+
+create policy "adoption_requests_select_own" on public.adoption_requests
+  for select to authenticated using ((select auth.uid()) = user_id);
fix.prompt: Lovable, please lock down the adoption_requests table in Supabase. Make sure row level security is enabled and replace any read policy that lets everyone or every signed-in user read all rows with one that only lets users read their own rows (where user_id = auth.uid()). Add it as a new migration.

findings.title: Anyone on the internet can call send-email

ghost_path.story: A customer walks up to the shop.
ghost_path.why: Every request starts here. The app cannot trust anything the visitor sends.
ghost_path.code: No code runs yet. The visitor only has what the public website gives them.

ghost_path.story: They show their ID at the guard desk and get a pass.
ghost_path.why: The pass is how the side door knows who is knocking.
ghost_path.code: The request carries the user's access token in the Authorization header.

ghost_path.story: At the side door send-email, the doorman reads the pass before letting them in.
ghost_path.why: Checking the pass on the server is the only check an attacker cannot skip.
ghost_path.code: The handler calls auth.getUser() and stops with 401 when there is no user.

ghost_path.data: only what this user may touch
ghost_path.story: Behind the door, they only reach api.resend.com on their own behalf.
ghost_path.why: Everything after the door acts for one known user.
ghost_path.code: The function uses api.resend.com for the checked user only.

attack_path.story: Someone with bad intentions walks around the back of the shop.
attack_path.why: Every request starts here. The app cannot trust anything the visitor sends.
attack_path.code: No code runs yet. The visitor only has what the public website gives them.

attack_path.data: a request with no pass at all
attack_path.story: The side door send-email has no doorman. They walk straight in.
attack_path.why: A Edge Function is reachable by anyone on the internet. Without a sign-in check, it works for strangers too.
attack_path.code: supabase/functions/send-email/index.ts line 2 starts handling the request without checking who sent it.

attack_path.story: The sign that says 'staff only' has been taken down.
attack_path.why: verify_jwt = false tells Supabase not to require a signed-in token before running the function.
attack_path.code: supabase/config.toml line 5 turns off the platform's own token check.

attack_path.story: From inside, they use api.resend.com as if they were the shop.
attack_path.why: Everything behind the door trusts that the door already checked.
attack_path.code: The function reaches api.resend.com with the app's own credentials.

fix.explanation: Anyone on the internet can call send-email, signed in or not. Add a check at the start of the handler that asks Supabase who the user is and stops with a 401 error when nobody is signed in, and turn verify_jwt back on.
fix.diff:
--- a/supabase/functions/send-email/index.ts
+++ b/supabase/functions/send-email/index.ts
@@ -0,0 +1,1 @@
+import { createClient } from 'npm:@supabase/supabase-js@2'
@@ -2,0 +4,7 @@
+  const authClient = createClient(
+    Deno.env.get('SUPABASE_URL')!,
+    Deno.env.get('SUPABASE_ANON_KEY')!,
+    { global: { headers: { Authorization: req.headers.get('Authorization') ?? '' } } },
+  )
+  const { data: { user } } = await authClient.auth.getUser()
+  if (!user) return new Response('Unauthorized', { status: 401 })
--- a/supabase/config.toml
+++ b/supabase/config.toml
@@ -5,1 +5,1 @@
-verify_jwt = false
+verify_jwt = true
fix.prompt: Lovable, please make send-email require a signed-in user. At the start of the handler, call supabase.auth.getUser() with the request's Authorization header and return a 401 error if there is no user. Do not turn off JWT verification for it.

findings.title: Anyone can make ai-describe spend your OpenAI credits

ghost_path.story: A customer walks up to the shop.
ghost_path.why: Every request starts here. The app cannot trust anything the visitor sends.
ghost_path.code: No code runs yet. The visitor only has what the public website gives them.

ghost_path.story: They show their ID at the guard desk and get a pass.
ghost_path.why: The pass is how the side door knows who is knocking.
ghost_path.code: The request carries the user's access token in the Authorization header.

ghost_path.story: At the side door ai-describe, the doorman reads the pass before letting them in.
ghost_path.why: Checking the pass on the server is the only check an attacker cannot skip.
ghost_path.code: The handler calls auth.getUser() and stops with 401 when there is no user.

ghost_path.data: only what this user may touch
ghost_path.story: Behind the door, they only reach api.openai.com on their own behalf.
ghost_path.why: Everything after the door acts for one known user.
ghost_path.code: The function uses api.openai.com for the checked user only.

attack_path.story: Someone with bad intentions finds the side door, with a script that knocks thousands of times.
attack_path.why: Every request starts here. The app cannot trust anything the visitor sends.
attack_path.code: No code runs yet. The visitor only has what the public website gives them.

attack_path.data: a request from a stranger, repeated without limit
attack_path.story: The side door ai-describe lets anyone in and runs to the supplier for every knock.
attack_path.why: Each call costs money. With no sign-in and no limit, a stranger decides how much you spend.
attack_path.code: supabase/functions/ai-describe/index.ts line 5 calls OpenAI for every request, with no user check and no rate limit.

attack_path.data: a paid request on your account
attack_path.story: Across the road, OpenAI bills you for every order.
attack_path.why: The provider charges the key's owner, which is you.
attack_path.code: Requests to OpenAI use the app's own key from the function secrets.

fix.explanation: Anyone can call ai-describe, and every call spends your OpenAI credits. Require a signed-in user before the paid call, and keep a small usage table so each user gets at most 20 calls an hour. Requests over the limit get a 429 error.
fix.diff:
--- a/supabase/functions/ai-describe/index.ts
+++ b/supabase/functions/ai-describe/index.ts
@@ -0,0 +1,1 @@
+import { createClient } from 'npm:@supabase/supabase-js@2'
@@ -4,0 +6,15 @@
+  const authClient = createClient(
+    Deno.env.get('SUPABASE_URL')!,
+    Deno.env.get('SUPABASE_ANON_KEY')!,
+    { global: { headers: { Authorization: req.headers.get('Authorization') ?? '' } } },
+  )
+  const { data: { user } } = await authClient.auth.getUser()
+  if (!user) return new Response('Unauthorized', { status: 401 })
+  const since = new Date(Date.now() - 60 * 60 * 1000).toISOString()
+  const { count } = await authClient
+    .from('ai_usage')
+    .select('id', { count: 'exact', head: true })
+    .eq('user_id', user.id)
+    .gte('created_at', since)
+  if ((count ?? 0) >= 20) return new Response('Too many requests', { status: 429 })
+  await authClient.from('ai_usage').insert({ user_id: user.id })
--- /dev/null
+++ b/supabase/migrations/0004_heist_ai_usage.sql
@@ -0,0 +1,12 @@
+create table public.ai_usage (
+  id bigint generated always as identity primary key,
+  user_id uuid not null default auth.uid() references auth.users(id),
+  created_at timestamptz not null default now()
+);
+
+alter table public.ai_usage enable row level security;
+
+create policy "ai_usage_select_own" on public.ai_usage
+  for select to authenticated using ((select auth.uid()) = user_id);
+create policy "ai_usage_insert_own" on public.ai_usage
+  for insert to authenticated with check ((select auth.uid()) = user_id);
fix.prompt: Lovable, please protect ai-describe. Before it calls OpenAI, require a signed-in user with supabase.auth.getUser() and return 401 if there is none. Then add a per-user limit of 20 calls per hour, tracked in a new ai_usage table with row level security, and return 429 when a user goes over it.

ghost_path.story: They show their ID at the guard desk and get a pass.

attack_path.story: They get a real pass at the guard desk. Nothing looks wrong yet.

attack_path.why: The anon key and table names are public by design. The lock is what keeps data safe.
attack_path.code: from('pets') reveals that the app reads pets.

attack_path.data: the public anon key, no account
attack_path.story: They walk right past the guard desk. Nobody asks who they are.
attack_path.why: Signing in only helps if the vault checks the pass. Here it does not.
attack_path.code: The public anon key alone is enough, so Supabase Auth is never involved.

attack_path.data: a lock that opens for everyone
attack_path.story: Here is the broken lock: it opens for anyone at all.
attack_path.why: A read policy must compare the row's owner with the user. This one does not.
attack_path.code: Policy pets_select_all on pets lets every visitor read every row.

attack_path.story: Every box in pets swings open, not just their own.
attack_path.why: Without an owner check, one query returns everyone's records.
attack_path.code: A plain select on pets returns all rows.

fix.explanation: The read rule on pets lets anyone read every row. If this table is meant to be public, nothing needs to change. If not, add a new migration that turns the lock on, then add a rule that says who may read each row.
fix.diff:
--- /dev/null
+++ b/supabase/migrations/0004_heist_lock_pets.sql
@@ -0,0 +1,5 @@
+drop policy "pets_select_all" on public.pets;
+
+-- Add a policy that says who may read each row, for example:
+-- create policy "pets_select_own" on public.pets
+--   for select to authenticated using ((select auth.uid()) = user_id);
fix.prompt: Lovable, if the pets table is not meant to be public, please lock down the pets table in Supabase. Make sure row level security is enabled and replace any read policy that lets everyone or every signed-in user read all rows with one that only lets users read their own rows. Add it as a new migration.

findings.title: Nobody can use files in id-documents yet. Add access rules instead of making it public

ghost_path.story: A customer walks up to the shop.
ghost_path.why: Every request starts here. The app cannot trust anything the visitor sends.
ghost_path.code: No code runs yet. The visitor only has what the public website gives them.

ghost_path.story: In the shop window, the customer hands over a file to store.
ghost_path.why: The browser sends files straight to storage, so storage must check who sends them.
ghost_path.code: from('id-documents') uploads to the id-documents bucket.

ghost_path.story: They show their ID at the guard desk first.
ghost_path.why: Storage rules use the signed-in user to decide who owns each file.
ghost_path.code: auth.uid() is available to storage.objects policies.

ghost_path.story: In the warehouse, they can reach only their own shelf in id-documents.
ghost_path.why: Per-user folders keep one customer's files away from another's.
ghost_path.code: A storage.objects policy limits id-documents to the user's own folder.

attack_path.story: Someone with bad intentions walks up to the same shop.
attack_path.why: Every request starts here. The app cannot trust anything the visitor sends.
attack_path.code: No code runs yet. The visitor only has what the public website gives them.

attack_path.story: The shop window shows which warehouse the files go to.
attack_path.why: Bucket names are public. The rules on storage.objects are the real lock.
attack_path.code: from('id-documents') names the id-documents bucket in its upload call.

attack_path.story: The id-documents warehouse has no rules posted. Right now nobody can use it, so the quick fix people reach for is propping the door open.
attack_path.why: Without storage.objects policies, the app cannot store files safely, and making the bucket public would expose every file.
attack_path.code: supabase/migrations/0002_storage.sql line 5 creates id-documents as private with no storage.objects policies.

attack_path.story: No guard checks who owns which shelf.
attack_path.why: Without policies, storage has no idea which file belongs to which user.
attack_path.code: No storage.objects policy mentions this bucket, so auth.uid() is never checked.

fix.explanation: id-documents is private but has no access rules, so the app cannot use it yet. Add rules that let each signed-in user read and upload only their own folder, instead of making the bucket public.
fix.diff:
--- /dev/null
+++ b/supabase/migrations/0004_heist_storage_id_documents.sql
@@ -0,0 +1,7 @@
+create policy "id_documents_read_own" on storage.objects
+  for select to authenticated
+  using (bucket_id = 'id-documents' and (select auth.uid())::text = (storage.foldername(name))[1]);
+
+create policy "id_documents_upload_own" on storage.objects
+  for insert to authenticated
+  with check (bucket_id = 'id-documents' and (select auth.uid())::text = (storage.foldername(name))[1]);
fix.prompt: Lovable, please add Supabase storage policies for the id-documents bucket. Each signed-in user should only read and upload files in a folder named after their user id. Store uploads under that folder and add the rules as a new migration.
